sections.text:
James is practical from the first line. It speaks about trials, about hearing God’s word and doing it, about treating rich and poor alike, and about the power of the tongue. It warns the wealthy who exploit workers and ends with patience, prayer for the sick and bringing back those who wander.

Its best-known argument is that faith without works is dead: real faith shows itself in what a person does.

Tradition identifies the author as James, the brother of Jesus and leader of the church in Jerusalem. The letter is addressed to Jewish Christians scattered abroad and echoes the teaching of Jesus closely. Some date it very early, in the 40s; others later.

James 2 seems at first to contradict Paul, who says people are made right with God by faith and not by works. Luther was uneasy with the letter for that reason. Most readers conclude that the two address different errors: Paul opposes earning God’s favor, James opposes a faith that is only words. The instruction to anoint the sick with oil (5:14) is practiced in different ways across churches.
